OPINION
Representing the Parties:
For Appellant: W. Byrd
For Respondent: Lawrence Xiao, Attorney
S. KIM, Administrative Law Judge: Pursuant to Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC)
section 19045, W. Byrd (appellant) appeals an action by respondent Franchise Tax Board (FTB)
proposing tax of $3,961 and applicable interest for the 2020 tax year.
Appellant elected to have this appeal determined pursuant to the procedures of the
Small Case Program. Those procedures require the assignment of a single panel member.
(Cal. Code Regs., tit. 18, § 30209.05(b).)
Appellant waived the right to an oral hearing; therefore, the matter was submitted to the
Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) on the written record pursuant to California Code of Regulations,
title 18, section 30209(a).
ISSUE
Whether appellant has established a basis to abate interest.1
FACTUAL FINDINGS
1. Appellant timely filed a 2020 California Resident Income Tax Return reporting state
wages but no federal adjusted gross income (AGI) or California AGI. Appellant also
reported taxable income of $4,601 and total tax of $4,389. After applying a withholding
credit of $4,409, appellant claimed an overpayment of $20. Appellant used an address
in Oakland, California (Oakland Address) on the tax return.
1 Appellant does not dispute the proposed amount of tax.

2. Since appellant did not report a California AGI and appellant’s reported taxable income
of $4,601 was below California’s minimum filing requirement, FTB issued appellant a
refund of $4,409, the entire withholding amount.
3. Subsequently, FTB obtained information from the IRS indicating that appellant’s federal
AGI was the same amount as appellant’s reported state wages. Based on that
information, on September 4, 2024, FTB issued appellant a Notice of Proposed
Assessment (NPA) proposing tax of $3,961 plus accrued interest. FTB sent the NPA to
appellant at the Oakland Address.
4. On November 1, 2024, appellant protested the NPA.
5. On May 1, 2025, FTB issued appellant a position letter requesting a response within
30 days. FTB sent the position letter to appellant at the Oakland Address. Appellant did
not respond.
6. On July 1, 2025, FTB issued appellant a letter indicating it did not receive a response.
FTB sent the letter to appellant at the Oakland Address.
7. On September 10, 2025, FTB issued appellant a letter denying interest abatement and a
Notice of Action (NOA) affirming the NPA. FTB sent both the letter and the NOA to
appellant at the Oakland Address.
8. Appellant timely filed this appeal.
DISCUSSION
Tax is due on the original due date of a return without regard to any filing extension.
(R&TC, § 19001.) If any amount of tax is not paid by the due date, interest is required to be
imposed from the due date until the date the taxes are paid. (R&TC, § 19101(a).) Interest is
not a penalty but is merely compensation for a taxpayer’s use of money after it should have
been paid to the state. (Appeal of Gorin, 2020-OTA-018P.) The imposition of interest is
mandatory, and interest can only be abated in certain limited situations when authorized by law.
(Appeal of Balch, 2018-OTA-159P.) There is no reasonable cause exception to the imposition
of interest. (Appeal of Gorin, supra.)
Appeal of Byrd 2

Generally, to obtain interest relief, the taxpayer must qualify under R&TC
sections 19104, 19112, or 21012.2 Under R&TC section 19104, FTB may abate interest related
to an proposed assessment to the extent that interest is attributable in whole or in part to any
unreasonable error or delay by an officer or employee of FTB when performing a ministerial or
managerial act, which occurred after FTB contacted the taxpayer in writing regarding the
proposed assessment, provided that no significant aspect of that error or delay can be attributed
to the taxpayer. (R&TC, § 19104(a)(1), (b)(1); Appeal of Gorin, supra.)
OTA’s jurisdiction in an interest abatement case is limited, and OTA can only review
FTB’s determination for abuse of discretion. (R&TC, § 19104(b)(2)(B).) To show an abuse of
discretion, the taxpayer must establish that FTB exercised its discretion arbitrarily, capriciously,
or without sound basis in fact or law. (Appeal of Gorin, supra.) Generally, abatement of interest
is ordered only when denial would be widely perceived as grossly unfair. (Ibid.)
Here, appellant contends that interest should be abated because FTB mistakenly issued
appellant a refund and FTB did not issue its proposed assessment until more than three years
later. Appellant argues that, after filing his protest of the NPA on November 1, 2024, he did not
receive a response until FTB issued the NOA on September 10, 2025. Therefore, appellant
asserts that the interest is attributable to an unreasonable error and delay by FTB.
However, under R&TC section 19104, interest can only be relieved for periods which
occurred after FTB contacted appellant in writing regarding the proposed assessment. (R&TC,
§ 19104(b)(1).) Any period before FTB issued the NPA, specifically the time between the
issuance of the initial refund and the issuance of the NPA, does not qualify for interest relief
under R&TC section 19104. Moreover, FTB issued the initial refund based on amounts
appellant reported (or failed to report) on his 2020 tax return, and thus, a significant aspect of
the error can be attributed to appellant. (See R&TC, § 19104(b)(1).)
After appellant protested the NPA on November 1, 2024, FTB issued its position six
months later on May 1, 2025. After appellant failed to respond to the position letter, FTB issued
another letter on July 1, 2025, and then the NOA on September 10, 2025. A period of six
months can be a reasonable amount of time for FTB to issue a position letter in response to
appellant’s protest. (See Appeal of Gorin, supra.) Despite appellant’s assertion that he never
2 R&TC section 21012 allows FTB to abate interest where there was reasonable reliance on
written advice from FTB. Appellant has not shown that he relied on any written advice requested of FTB.
R&TC section 19112 also allows FTB to abate interest where an individual demonstrates inability to pay
interest solely because of extreme financial hardship caused by significant disability or other catastrophic
circumstance. However, OTA does not have the legal authority to review or overturn FTB’s denial of a
waiver of interest based on extreme financial hardship. (Appeal of Moy, 2019-OTA-057P.) Therefore,
neither of these provisions apply to this appeal.

received FTB’s letters, FTB mailed the letters to the Oakland Address appellant listed on his
2020 tax return. Any notice mailed to a taxpayer shall be sufficient if mailed to the taxpayer’s
last known address, or the address that appears on the taxpayer’s last return filed with FTB,
unless the taxpayer has provided the FTB clear and concise notification of a different address.
(R&TC, § 18416.) Furthermore, FTB mailed the NPA and NOA to the same Oakland Address,
and appellant received both notices.
Based on the foregoing, FTB did not abuse its discretion in denying appellant’s request
for interest abatement.
HOLDING
Appellant has not established a basis to abate interest.
DISPOSITION
FTB’s action is sustained.
Steven Kim
Administrative Law Judge
